title: What's the deal with Baby Boomers?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant (with guest producer Noel) explore the Baby Boomer generation: its definition (roughly 1946-1964), why birth rates spiked after World War II, the split between the "leading edge" boomers and the later "shadow boomers" or Generation Jones, and the shared experiences (JFK, moon landing, Vietnam, TV, rock and roll) that shaped them. They cover boomer consumerism, suburbanization and its effect on women, political views, their role in Social Security and retirement finances, work ethic claims, end-of-life preferences, and boomer cannabis use. Listener mail about British place-name pronunciation closes the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and generations
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode, joke about their own generations, and discuss why generations are defined by birth years and shared life experiences such as major events.

segments.title: Why the baby boom happened
segments.summary: The hosts explain the post-WWII surge in births, combining returning veterans, postwar prosperity optimism, and older parents who had delayed children during the Depression. Birth numbers rose through the 1950s and dipped after 1964, around when the pill became widely available.

segments.title: Boomer identity and Kathleen Casey Kirschling
segments.summary: The boomers' cultural arc is outlined, from the 1960s youth movement to the 1970s excess and 1980s yuppies, and later volunteerism. Kathleen Casey Kirschling, regarded as the first baby boomer, born just after midnight on January 1, 1946 in New Jersey, is profiled as a prototypical boomer.

segments.title: Boomer statistics and family living
segments.summary: The hosts review boomer statistics: the suburbs, consumerism, being the first children targeted by advertisers, state distribution, marriage rates, and expectations about adult children moving back home and parents moving in.

segments.title: Boomers and the millennial population comparison
segments.summary: Millennials surpassed boomers in population around 2015, with about 74 million versus 74.9 million boomers. Boomers peaked at about 78.8 million, and the hosts note that the millennial generation is expected to peak next year.

segments.title: Splitting boomers: leading edge vs. Generation Jones
segments.summary: Boomers born roughly 1946-1954 are the leading edge, while those born 1955-1964 are called shadow boomers or Generation Jones. The later group had high expectations but fewer resources and is described as more cynical. Howard Schuman and Jacqueline Scott's mid-1980s research is discussed, contrasting the leading edge's JFK, MLK, and Vietnam experiences with Nixon, Watergate, the Cold War, and the oil embargo.

segments.title: Shared events, disasters, and TV
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether generations need a disaster to unite them, personal memories of Challenger and the Reagan shooting, and sociologist Karl Mannheim's theory that generations are bound by shared experience. Television is presented as a way for a generation to share the same news and culture at the same time, along with rock and roll and skepticism toward authority.

segments.title: Boomer contradictions, politics, and consumerism
segments.summary: The hosts discuss boomers as both selfless and selfish, shifting from the 1960s activism to 1980s consumerism. A 2004 AP poll found boomers supported abortion rights, gun control, and stem cell research but also the death penalty and fiscal conservatism. A Gallup figure on self-reported ideology is mentioned. The boomers' embrace of spending on oneself is contrasted with the Depression-era generation's thrift.

segments.title: Boomer presidents
segments.summary: Bill Clinton and George W. Bush are identified as the first two boomer presidents, both born in 1946. Barack Obama is placed in Generation Jones, and Donald Trump is said to be born in 1946 as well, though the hosts' statement on the latter is partly garbled. Joe Biden's comments about running again are mentioned.

segments.title: Boomers, aging, healthcare, and Social Security
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the boomers' aging as a demographic bulge that will raise demand for elder services and healthcare. Boomers are described as health-conscious, with jogging and vegetarian diets. A digression about Chris Farley and butter on steak follows. The Social Security trust fund, a reserve fund of about $2.6 trillion, is described as becoming depleted, with projected benefits near 78 percent. Options for shoring it up are noted, and the 2008 recession's effect on boomer retirement savings is discussed.

segments.title: Boomer retirement finances and work ethic
segments.summary: Many boomers cannot retire and must keep working, though some work by choice. The hosts give personal financial advice to younger people. Keith Zabel's study of work ethic across generations found no meaningful difference, though boomers may prefer hierarchical structures. Statistics from a Motley Fool survey are cited on boomers relying on Social Security and lacking savings.

segments.title: Boomer end-of-life, suburbs, feminism, and cannabis
segments.summary: The hosts discuss boomers' preference for cremation and celebratory funerals, and the 1950s suburban boom's effect on women, referencing Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique and the rise of second-wave feminism. They then discuss Benjamin Han's study on rising cannabis use among older adults from 2006 to 2013, and an anecdote about older hippies at a South Carolina island retreat.

segments.title: Listener mail: English place-name pronunciation
segments.summary: A listener, Ian Rose, corrects the hosts on the pronunciation of Hertfordshire, Leicestershire (Loughborough is pronounced Luffborough), and notes that Cambridge is in Cambridgeshire, not Hertfordshire.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and point them to the show's social media, email, and website.
